summary.text: A universal series $F$ satisfying $xF'(x)=-(\sum_{r\ge1}\sigma_2(r)x^r)F(x)$ is used to identify the desired term as $[x^m]F(x)^m$. For $\Phi=F(x)^p/F(x^p)$, the divisor-sum identity gives $v_p([x^t]\log\Phi)\ge v_p(t)+1$; expanding $\Phi^M$ exponentially, bounding the factorial denominators for $p\ge3$, and estimating the linear convolution yields divisibility by $p^{2v_p(M)+2}$, after which $M=np^{k-1}$ gives the result.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(N)=[X^N]\prod_{r=1}^{N}(1-X^r)^{Nr}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\ge 3\) and all positive integers \(n,k\),
\[
A(np^k)\equiv A(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{2k}}.
\]

Throughout the proof, \(\sigma_2(m)=\sum_{d\mid m}d^2\). We use formal power series over \(\mathbb Z\) or \(\mathbb Q\), so all infinite products below are understood coefficientwise: the coefficient of any fixed power of \(X\) depends on only finitely many factors.

Define
\[
F(X)=\prod_{r\ge 1}(1-X^r)^r\in\mathbb Z[[X]].
\]
Its constant term is \(1\). For every positive integer \(N\), factors with \(r>N\) cannot affect the coefficient of \(X^N\), and hence
\[
[X^N]F(X)^N
=[X^N]\prod_{r=1}^{N}(1-X^r)^{Nr}
=A(N).                                                    \tag{1}
\]
Thus the sequence in the problem is the diagonal sequence \([X^N]F^N\).

We first record the logarithmic derivative of \(F\). For one factor,
\[
X\frac{d}{dX}\log(1-X^r)^r
=-\frac{r^2X^r}{1-X^r}
=-r^2\sum_{j\ge1}X^{rj}.
\]
After summing over \(r\), the coefficient of \(X^m\) is
\(-\sum_{r\mid m}r^2=-\sigma_2(m)\). Therefore, if
\[
E(X)=\sum_{m\ge1}\sigma_2(m)X^m,
\]
then
\[
XF'(X)=-E(X)F(X).                                         \tag{2}
\]
More generally, for every positive integer \(M\),
\[
X(F^M)'=-M E F^M.                                         \tag{3}
\]
Writing
\[
c_M(j)=[X^j]F(X)^M,
\]
and comparing the coefficient of \(X^\ell\) in (3), for \(\ell\ge1\), gives
\[
\ell c_M(\ell)
=-M\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}\sigma_2(t)c_M(\ell-t).              \tag{4}
\]
Every \(c_M(j)\) is an integer because \(F^M\in\mathbb Z[[X]]\).

Fix from now on a prime \(p\ge3\). For a nonzero rational number \(q\), write \(v_p(q)\) for its \(p\)-adic valuation. Statements that a coefficient has valuation at least some integer are also understood to hold when that coefficient is zero.

If \(M\ge1\), put
\[
\alpha=v_p(M).
\]
Equation (4), together with the integrality of every term in its sum, gives the useful estimate
\[
v_p(c_M(\ell))\ge \alpha-v_p(\ell)\qquad(\ell\ge1).       \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, the sum on the right of (4) is an integer, so its valuation is at least zero; division by \(\ell\) then proves (5). We will also use the weaker but always valid fact
\[
v_p(c_M(\ell))\ge0                                       \tag{6}
\]
coming directly from integrality.

We next compare \(F(X)^p\) with \(F(X^p)\). Define the unit
\[
\Phi(X)=\frac{F(X)^p}{F(X^p)}\in\mathbb Q[[X]].            \tag{7}
\]
Both numerator and denominator have constant term \(1\), so \(\Phi(0)=1\). From (2), applied both to \(F(X)\) and to \(F(X^p)\), we obtain
\[
X\frac{\Phi'}{\Phi}
=p\bigl(E(X^p)-E(X)\bigr).
\]
Set
\[
B(X)=p\bigl(E(X^p)-E(X)\bigr)=\sum_{t\ge1}B_tX^t.         \tag{8}
\]
Thus
\[
X\Phi'=B\Phi.                                             \tag{9}
\]
Explicitly,
\[
B_t=p\left({\bf1}_{p\mid t}\,\sigma_2(t/p)-\sigma_2(t)\right).  \tag{10}
\]

The crucial divisibility of \(B_t\) follows from multiplicativity of \(\sigma_2\). If \(t=p^r u\), where \(r=v_p(t)\) and \(p\nmid u\), then
\[
\sigma_2(t)=(1+p^2+\cdots+p^{2r})\sigma_2(u).
\]
If \(r\ge1\), similarly
\[
\sigma_2(t/p)=(1+p^2+\cdots+p^{2(r-1)})\sigma_2(u),
\]
so (10) becomes
\[
B_t=-p^{2r+1}\sigma_2(u).
\]
When \(r=0\), (10) gives \(B_t=-p\sigma_2(t)\), which is the same divisibility assertion. Consequently,
\[
p^{2v_p(t)+1}\mid B_t                                  \tag{11}
\]
for every \(t\ge1\).

Define a formal power series with zero constant term by
\[
\Psi(X)=\sum_{t\ge1}\frac{B_t}{t}X^t.                    \tag{12}
\]
Then
\[
X\Psi'(X)=B(X).                                           \tag{13}
\]
By (11),
\[
v_p([X^t]\Psi)=v_p(B_t/t)
\ge 2v_p(t)+1-v_p(t)=v_p(t)+1\qquad(t\ge1).               \tag{14}
\]
In particular, every coefficient of \(\Psi\) has valuation at least \(1\):
\[
v_p([X^t]\Psi)\ge1.                                     \tag{15}
\]

Equations (9) and (13), together with \(\Phi(0)=1\) and \(\Psi(0)=0\), imply
\[
\Phi(X)=\exp(\Psi(X)).                                    \tag{16}
\]
For completeness, this identity can be seen without any analytic argument. Both sides have constant term \(1\), and both satisfy the same formal differential equation \(XY'=BY\); comparison of the coefficient of \(X^m\), proceeding inductively in \(m\), uniquely determines every coefficient from the earlier ones. It follows that, for every nonnegative integer \(M\),
\[
\Phi(X)^M=\exp(M\Psi(X))
=\sum_{d\ge0}\frac{M^d}{d!}\Psi(X)^d.                   \tag{17}
\]
Since \(\Psi\) has zero constant term, only terms with \(d\le b\) can contribute to the coefficient of \(X^b\).

We now estimate the nonlinear part of (17). Put
\[
R_M(X)=\Phi(X)^M-1-M\Psi(X)
=\sum_{d\ge2}\frac{M^d}{d!}\Psi(X)^d.                    \tag{18}
\]
By (15), every coefficient of \(\Psi^d\) has valuation at least \(d\): each coefficient is a finite sum of products of \(d\) coefficients of \(\Psi\), and every such product has valuation at least \(d\).

We also need the elementary factorial estimate
\[
v_p(d!)\le d-2\qquad(d\ge2,\ p\ge3).                    \tag{19}
\]
One way to prove it is to use Legendre's formula
\[
(p-1)v_p(d!)=d-s_p(d),
\]
where \(s_p(d)\) is the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(d\). Since \(d\ge1\), we have \(s_p(d)\ge1\), and since \(p-1\ge2\),
\(2v_p(d!)\le d-1\). For \(d=2\) this forces \(v_p(2!)=0\); for \(d\ge3\), it implies \(v_p(d!)\le d-2\). This proves (19).

For every \(d\ge2\), every coefficient of the corresponding summand in (18) therefore has valuation at least
\[
d\alpha+d-v_p(d!)
\ge d\alpha+2
\ge2\alpha+2.                                             \tag{20}
\]
The nonarchimedean inequality says that a finite sum of rationals each having valuation at least \(2\alpha+2\) again has valuation at least \(2\alpha+2\). Hence every coefficient of \(R_M\) satisfies
\[
v_p([X^b]R_M)\ge2\alpha+2\qquad(b\ge0).                 \tag{21}
\]
(The constant coefficient is actually zero.)

We now prove the central one-step congruence
\[
A(Mp)\equiv A(M)\pmod {p^{2v_p(M)+2}}                    \tag{22}
\]
for every positive integer \(M\).

Let
\[
C(X)=F(X)^M=\sum_{j\ge0}c_M(j)X^j.
\]
From the definition of \(\Phi\),
\[
F(X)^{Mp}=F(X^p)^M\Phi(X)^M=C(X^p)\Phi(X)^M.              \tag{23}
\]
Using (1),
\[
A(Mp)=[X^{Mp}]C(X^p)\Phi(X)^M.                            \tag{24}
\]
Also,
\[
A(M)=[X^M]C(X)=[X^{Mp}]C(X^p).                            \tag{25}
\]
Subtracting (25) from (24), and using
\(\Phi^M-1=R_M+M\Psi\), gives
\[
A(Mp)-A(M)
=[X^{Mp}]C(X^p)R_M
+M[X^{Mp}]C(X^p)\Psi.                                     \tag{26}
\]

Consider the first term on the right. Every coefficient of \(C(X^p)\) is an integer, hence has nonnegative \(p\)-adic valuation, while every coefficient of \(R_M\) has valuation at least \(2\alpha+2\) by (21). Every product in the coefficient convolution therefore has valuation at least \(2\alpha+2\), and so
\[
v_p\bigl([X^{Mp}]C(X^p)R_M\bigr)\ge2\alpha+2.            \tag{27}
\]

It remains to control the linear term in \(\Psi\). We claim
\[
v_p\bigl([X^{Mp}]C(X^p)\Psi\bigr)\ge\alpha+2.            \tag{28}
\]
The only nonzero coefficients of \(C(X^p)\) occur in degrees \(p\ell\), where the coefficient is \(c_M(\ell)\). Thus a term in the convolution for the coefficient of \(X^{Mp}\) has the form
\[
c_M(\ell)\,[X^b]\Psi,
\qquad p\ell+b=Mp.
\]
Necessarily \(0\le\ell\le M\) and
\[
b=p(M-\ell).                                              \tag{29}
\]
If \(\ell=M\), then \(b=0\), and this term vanishes because \(\Psi(0)=0\). We may therefore assume \(\ell<M\). Put
\[
\gamma=v_p(M-\ell).
\]
Then (29) and the stronger estimate (14) give
\[
v_p([X^b]\Psi)\ge v_p(b)+1=\gamma+2.                    \tag{30}
\]
There are two cases.

First suppose \(\alpha\le\gamma\). Since \(c_M(\ell)\) is an integer, (6) and (30) give
\[
v_p\bigl(c_M(\ell)[X^b]\Psi\bigr)
\ge0+\gamma+2\ge\alpha+2.                                \tag{31}
\]

Now suppose \(\alpha>\gamma\). In this case \(\ell\ne0\), and
\[
v_p(\ell)=\gamma.                                        \tag{32}
\]
Indeed, \(p^{\gamma+1}\) divides \(M\), whereas it does not divide \(M-\ell\). Since \(\ell=M-(M-\ell)\), it follows that \(p^\gamma\mid\ell\) but \(p^{\gamma+1}\nmid\ell\), proving (32). Applying (5) and (30), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p\bigl(c_M(\ell)[X^b]\Psi\bigr)
&\ge (\alpha-v_p(\ell))+(\gamma+2)\\
&=(\alpha-\gamma)+(\gamma+2)=\alpha+2.
\end{aligned}                                             \tag{33}
\]
Thus every summand in the convolution has valuation at least \(\alpha+2\), proving (28).

Multiplication by \(M\) adds \(\alpha=v_p(M)\) to the valuation in (28). Therefore
\[
v_p\left(M[X^{Mp}]C(X^p)\Psi\right)\ge2\alpha+2.         \tag{34}
\]
Combining (26), (27), and (34), we conclude that the integer \(A(Mp)-A(M)\) has \(p\)-adic valuation at least \(2\alpha+2\). Equivalently,
\[
p^{2v_p(M)+2}\mid A(Mp)-A(M),
\]
which is exactly the one-step congruence (22).

Finally, let \(n,k\ge1\), and set
\[
M=np^{k-1}.
\]
Then \(M\ge1\), \(Mp=np^k\), and
\[
v_p(M)=v_p(n)+k-1\ge k-1.
\]
Applying (22) gives
\[
p^{2v_p(M)+2}\mid A(np^k)-A(np^{k-1}).
\]
Since
\[
2v_p(M)+2\ge2(k-1)+2=2k,
\]
we also have
\[
p^{2k}\mid A(np^k)-A(np^{k-1}).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{A(np^k)\equiv A(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{2k}}}
\]
for every prime \(p\ge3\) and all positive integers \(n,k\), as required.
